Photograph: Carlos Osorio/AP House of Representatives US representative Marcy Kaptur taken to hospital after car crash Toledo police say Ohio Democrat is active and alert after two-vehicle hit-and-run collision on Sunday Reuters Sun 2 Aug 2026 16.20 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Marcy Kaptur is being treated ⁠for non-life-threatening injuries after a car crash in Toledo, ⁠ Ohio , on Sunday, ⁠the ​ Democratic US representative’s office said. Kaptur, 80, was a passenger ⁠in the vehicle and on her way to church, her office ⁠said. Toledo police did not ​respond to ‌a request from Reuters for ‌comment. But the department told local news ‌outlets that officers responded to a two-vehicle crash shortly before 11am local time. Police described it as a hit-and-run, also sometimes known as a “hit-skip” incident, and was taken to the hospital, multiple outlets reported. Kaptur represents Ohio’s ninth congressional district and has been in the US House of Representatives for 43 years. “She is ‌active, alert, and being treated for non-life-threatening injuries,” Kaptur’s office ​said in a statement. She is the longest-serving ⁠female lawmaker in the history of the ​chamber, ​according to House ​records. She is seeking re-election in ​the ‌fall against ​Derek ​Merrin, a Republican former member of the Ohio legislature. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Around 2-3 times a day Sign up to Breaking News US Get the most important news as it breaks Preview latest after newsletter promotion The district includes parts of Toledo and stretches across north-western Ohio along the southern shore of Lake Erie. She was born in Toledo and before becoming an elected politician herself she worked in urban planning and advised Jimmy Carter’s administration. https://www.nbcnews.com/world/ukraine/ru.text: Russia pounded the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, and the surrounding region with scores of missiles and drones in a nighttime aerial attack that lasted for hours and killed at least 14 people, officials said Thursday. Moscow’s forces have in recent months intensified their ballistic missile attacks on Kyiv, exploiting Ukraine’s chronic shortage of U.S.-made Patriot air defense interceptors, the sole weapon in its arsenal able to shoot down ballistic missiles. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has pleaded for countries to send more Patriot interceptors, but international stockpiles are low amid the Iran war and Ukraine’s more than four-year fight against Russia’s all-out invasion. Russia’s overnight barrage also included cruise missiles and fast-flying, jet-powered drones that put further strain on air defenses, the Ukrainian air force said. Explosions boomed across the city in the dark. Kyiv was the primary target, but hits were recorded at 28 locations across the country, according to the air force. About 40 people were wounded, Zelenskyy said, as air raid warnings remained in place until after dawn. Russia and Ukraine have battered each other with drones and missiles as their armies struggle to gain the upper hand on the 780-mile front line, where huge numbers of drones are pinning down troops. Ukraine has attempted to shift the war onto Russian soil through long-range drone strikes on oil facilities and other infrastructure. The Russian Defense Ministry said Thursday morning that air defenses shot down 726 Ukrainian drones overnight over a number of Russian regions, annexed Crimea and the Black and Azov seas, in one of Ukraine’s biggest aerial attacks of the war. There were no immediate reports of damage or casualties. Russia’s relentless onslaught on Kyiv has spooked other European countries, especially those bordering Ukraine, which fear what Russian President Vladimir Putin might have in store for the continent. As the Russian attack on Kyiv unfolded, the Polish Armed Forces Operational Command activated its military aviation operations, ground-based air defense systems and its radar reconnaissance. Polish and other NATO military aircraft were deployed to monitor the country’s airspace, Polish news agency PAP reported. Romania’s Defense Ministry said that an unidentified drone crashed and caught fire in an uninhabited area near the border with Ukraine. Two Spanish F-18 jets, deployed on an air policing mission in Romania, were scrambled after 2 a.m. local time to monitor a group of “air targets” near the border, the ministry said. Also, Moldova’s Defense Ministry said that its airspace was breached by an unauthorized drone. Russia’s overnight strikes hit 12 locations across Kyiv’s Darnytskyi, Sviatoshynskyi and Solomianskyi districts, damaging residential buildings, a medical facility and an educational institution. Emergency crews were at the scene and pulled people out from under the rubble. Larysa Bondaruk, 60, sat on the ground, holding her cat, Chanel, which had been rescued by firefighters. With tears in her eyes, she said that her neighbor’s grandson had been trapped under the rubble and died. Her apartment was badly damaged. “A rocket hit the roof. It was incredibly loud. Immediately, debris and doors were blown out. There were columns of smoke, columns of fire, screams, crying and despair,” she said. “Two people were killed in our building, but the rescuers responded quickly and professionally. I am grateful to them for that.” In Solomianskyi district, the top two floors of a nine-story residential building were destroyed, and fires broke out on other floors. People were also trapped in two residential buildings and a school shelter.

https://www.dw.com/en/why-eritrea-matter.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5NGTu For Eritrea's President Isaias Afwerki the end of US sanctions removes one source of international pressure [FILE: February 2023] Image: Khalil Senosi/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement On September 23, fighting escalated dramatically in Ethiopia 's Tigray region. Tigrayan forces seized three local airports and fighting spread into the neighboring regions of Afar and Amhara, according to reports. Both sides accuse the other of starting the escalation. The renewed fighting poses a major challenge to the 2022 Pretoria peace agreement that ended the previous Tigray war. This is where Eritrea becomes crucial. Martin Plaut, a British journalist specializing in the Horn of Africa , noted that the US needs Eritrea in the struggle to secure the Red Sea against the Houthis , an Iran-backed Shiite Muslim militia. Plaut argues that removing sanctions gives new political weight to one of Africa's most repressive regimes. As fighting resumes in Tigray , Eritrea could once again become a decisive military player. Plaut said that the current tensions had the potential of developing into a broader regional confrontation, which, he said, "is the most serious danger." In his view, US President Donald Trump's administration has already made a strategic calculation: "Trump has now mended fences with Eritrea and has lifted sanctions against Eritrea" in an effort to reduce the threat posed by the Houthis and secure the Red Sea. Eritrea's location at the Bab Al-Mandab Strait is an asset for the autocratic nation, as partners from near and far seek access to the Red Sea Image: ABACA/picture alliance A striking coincidence of timing The escalation in Tigray came only days after Washington removed key Eritrean entities and individuals from its sanctions list. On September 18, the United States allowed the national emergency underpinning its Ethiopia-related sanctions regime to expire. The Treasury Department subsequently removed a number of Eritrean individuals and entities from its sanctions list, including senior financial official Hagos Ghebrehiwet and the Red Sea Trading Corporation. The measures had originally been imposed in 2021 in connection with the Tigray war. US officials have not described the move as an endorsement of Eritrea, nor has Washington publicly said that it struck a deal with Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki . But it removes a layer of pressure on a government whose strategic importance has grown as security around the Red Sea deteriorates . For Abdurahman Sayed, director of the Horn of Africa Centre for Regional Integration and a political analyst, the wider geopolitical context is crucial. "It is happening at a time when the war on Iran is ongoing," he told DW. "The Strait of Hormuz has been blocked for some time , and now the Bab el-Mendeb on the Red Sea, where Eritrea is located, this may give Eritrea some advantage to establish a meaningful relationship with the US." Why Eritrea matters Eritrea controls a long coastline opposite Yemen . Its southern port of Assab lies close to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, one of the world's most important maritime chokepoints. Moses Okello, a senior researcher at the Institute for Security Studies in Addis Ababa, says the regional context has fundamentally changed since the previous Tigray war. "In 2020, the concern was the TPLF [Tigray People's Liberation Front] versus the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF)," he told DW. "Today, the entire Middle East is up in flames, and now the tensions in the Red Sea. So this changes the strategic value of not just the Eritrean coast, but the entire Red Sea waterway." Why northern Ethiopia is seeing growing violence once again To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video For Washington, cooperation — or at least non-hostility — from Eritrea can therefore be strategically valuable. But the bargain carries risks. Eritrea is one of the world's most authoritarian states, with no national elections since independence in 1993 and an extensive system of indefinite national service. Eritrean forces also fought alongside Ethiopian federal troops during the 2020-22 Tigray war. And the economic impact of lifting sanctions may be more limited than the political symbolism suggests. "Lifting the sanctions may not make a huge difference on the ground," said Sayed. "Eritrea is not a trade hub [nor does it have] a well-established trading relationship with the outside world. It's actually a closed country." Ethiopia heads back towards war The latest fighting did not emerge from nowhere. On September 21, seven Ethiopian armed and political groups announced an alliance aimed at removing Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government. The coalition includes the TPLF, the Amhara Fano National Movement and the Oromo Liberation Army. Some members were on opposing sides during the 2020-22 Tigray war. It remains unclear how closely the alliance's members will coordinate militarily. The alliance brings together groups with very different histories that share opposition to the federal government. Two days later, fighting escalated in Tigray. Tigrayan forces seized airports and fighting spread into neighboring regions. The TPLF says federal forces attacked first; Addis Ababa says the TPLF launched the offensive. The renewed fighting has raised questions about the durability of the 2022 Pretoria agreement. Could Eritrea intervene? During the previous Tigray war, Eritrean forces fought alongside Ethiopian federal troops. But relations between Afwerki and Abiy have since deteriorated sharply. One major dispute concerns Ethiopia's demand for reliable access to the Red Sea. Landlocked since Eritrea's independence, Ethiopia regards maritime access as a strategic necessity. Eritrea insists on its sovereignty and has rejected any suggestion that Ethiopia could obtain access through coercion. The new rebel alliance transforming the Tigray conflict To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The Ethiopian government has accused Eritrea of supporting armed groups in the new conflict. Eritrea denies such allegations. There is currently no public evidence that the US sanctions decision was designed to encourage Eritrean military intervention in Ethiopia. Nor is it clear that Asmara has decided to enter the fighting. But if the Tigray conflict intensifies , Eritrea could see a direct security interest in intervening. That would transform an Ethiopian conflict into a potentially interstate confrontation. A regional conflict waiting to spread The Horn of Africa is already exceptionally volatile. Sudan remains at war. Somalia is unstable. Ethiopia and Egypt remain locked in a dispute over the Nile and the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam. Saudi Arabia and the UAE are pursuing their own interests across the Red Sea and Horn of Africa. And the conflict in Yemen is directly connected to the security of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Okello sees the changing Middle East as an additional reason for urgent engagement. "There is no doubt that the conflict in the Middle East now puts a new contextual layer over that primary tension and increases the urgency to engage with both Eritrea and Addis Ababa to try and address this before it becomes a conflagration which makes addressing issues in the Red Sea a lot more difficult." A new Ethiopia-Eritrea confrontation would therefore not happen in isolation. Plaut warns that regional alliances could interact in dangerous ways. "You have the UAE backing the RSF and you have the Saudis backing the Eritreans and the Sudanese Armed Forces," he told DW. "This could all multiply and you could get one conflict leading into another." That does not mean a general regional war is inevitable. Most governments involved have strong reasons to prevent an uncontrollable escalation. But the number of links between the region's conflicts is increasing. Eritrea and shifting regional dynamics For Eritrea's President Afwerki, the US decision is an opportunity. The end of the sanctions removes one source of international pressure and may give Eritrea greater diplomatic room for maneuver. More importantly, Washington's renewed engagement with Asmara underscores the strategic value of Eritrea's Red Sea position. Why can't Ethiopia and Eritrea be friends? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The more important Eritrea becomes to US and regional security calculations, the greater the danger that strategic interests will overshadow concerns about its authoritarian system and past military interventions. For Ethiopia, the immediate question is whether the renewed fighting can be stopped before it draws in Eritrea. For Washington, the challenge is whether Eritrea can be engaged as a Red Sea security partner without giving Asmara greater freedom to destabilize its neighbors. Eritrea has spent decades on the margins of international diplomacy. Its location on the Red Sea has long given it strategic significance. With fighting again raging in Tigray, the Houthis threatening the Red Sea and Washington reopening its channel to Asmara, Eritrea could become one of the key players in the Horn of Africa's next chapter. Ekinder Firew in Addis Ababa contributed to this report. Audi confirmed on September 24 that a standard-production A6 Sportback e-tron Performance drove 1,338 km, or 831 miles, on a single charge, setting a Guinness World Record for the longest distance covered by a production EV without recharging. Rally driver Miko Marczyk did it in a car with the same 94.9 kWh battery and 367-hp powertrain sitting on dealer lots right now, not a stripped test mule with extra battery packs bolted in. That distinction matters for anyone cross-shopping the A6 e-tron against the Mercedes EQE, BMW i5 , or Genesis Electrified G80. The run averaged 7.09 kWh per 100 km, or 8.76 miles per kWh, which is nearly double the car's official WLTP efficiency rating. It's not a number regular owners will replicate on a Monday commute, but it does set a real ceiling for what this platform can squeeze out of a charge when every variable lines up. How Marczyk Pulled 831 Miles Out of a Car Rated for 483 Audi Marczyk, the 2025 FIA European Rally Champion, started the attempt at 1:55 a.m. on September 11 in Poland, tracing the Vistula River through Kraków, Sandomierz, Warsaw, Toruń, and Grudziądz before reaching Hel on the Baltic coast and turning back. The car finally ran dry between Toruń and Ciechocinek, 45 hours and 1,338 km after leaving. Audi says the drive happened in regular traffic, including rush hour, at an average ambient temperature around 15°C, dipping to 7°C overnight. The A6 Sportback e-tron Performance carries an official WLTP range of up to 777 km (483 miles). Marczyk's run beat that by 561 km, or roughly 72%. He got there the old-fashioned way: steady speeds, anticipatory driving, careful tire pressure, and heavy use of regenerative braking, which the car can run up to 220 kW and which Audi says covers about 95% of everyday braking events without touching the mechanical brakes. The Real Story Is the Shape, Not the Battery Audi A6 Sportback e-Tron Audi Audi points to the A6 Sportback e-tron's 0.21 drag coefficient, the lowest of any Audi ever built, as the biggest factor behind the result. The company says aerodynamic drag accounts for roughly 40% of the car's energy consumption in the WLTP cycle, which means a slippery shape pays off more as speeds climb. Underneath, the car uses Audi's Premium Platform Electric architecture with an 800-volt system and a 100 kWh gross, 94.9 kWh usable battery. That's the detail luxury EV shoppers should sit with: this wasn't a lightened or de-contented special. Audi says the test car still made 367 hp and hit 62 mph in 5.4 seconds, matching any A6 e-tron Performance you could order today. Marczyk himself called the 1,338 km figure "a pleasant surprise," crediting the interplay of the drivetrain, battery, and aerodynamics rather than any hidden hardware. How It Stacks Up Against Lucid, and What It Doesn't Prove Audi A6 Sportback e-Tron Audi The previous production-EV record belonged to a Lucid Air Grand Touring , which covered 749 miles between Switzerland and Germany in 2025. The Audi beat that by more than 80 miles, despite riding on a smaller usable battery than the Lucid's roughly 112 kWh pack. For buyers comparing the EQE, i5, and Electrified G80, that's a useful data point on how much efficiency Audi's PPE platform and aerodynamic package can extract relative to sheer battery size. Still, Audi never disclosed Marczyk's average speed, and the company's own framing makes clear this isn't a new everyday range figure. Highway driving at typical speeds, with climate control running, will land well short of 831 miles. What the record does confirm is a genuine efficiency ceiling, not a stripped-down PR stunt, which is a meaningfully different claim than most range records make. A Second Record for a Driver Who Collects Them Audi A6 Sportback e-Tron Audi This isn't Marczyk's first efficiency headline. In 2025 he drove a fourth-generation Skoda Superb 2.0 TDI a claimed 1,759 miles (2,831 km) on a single tank of diesel, averaging 2.6 liters per 100 km. He's now holding Guinness marks on both sides of the powertrain divide, which he framed as evidence that Volkswagen Group's EV technology has caught up to the diesel efficiency the brand built its reputation on for decades. For shoppers weighing the A6 e-tron against the EQE, i5, or Electrified G80 , the takeaway isn't that you'll see 800-plus miles on your own commute. It's that the platform has real headroom beyond its window-sticker number when aerodynamics and battery chemistry are both doing their job, which is a more useful benchmark than a lab test most owners will never approach anyway.
